title: Bartleby after
author: Salon
note: A mild refusal becomes the office’s true architecture—and pity learns the shape of its limits. After Melville, Bartleby, 1853.

scenes.title: Behind the screen
scenes.reentry: I am a man who believes in soft walls and quieter victories.

breaths.text: I am a man who believes in soft walls and quieter victories.
I manage a small corporate practice near Bryant Park: contracts, compliance language, the kind of work that pays without making a spectacle of anyone.
My associates were ordinary enough—useful in their weather—until I hired Bartleby.
He arrived pale, neat, almost weightless, with a résumé that said little and eyes that said less.
No LinkedIn.
No chatter in the lobby.
I placed him at a desk behind a folding screen, near the window that faced a brick air shaft and a slice of someone else’s fire escape.
He copied with a silent diligence that pleased me.
For three days I congratulated myself on the hire.
The printer hummed.
The city pressed its noise against the glass and failed to enter him.
On the fourth day I asked him to review a clause with me—ordinary work, the sort of second pair of eyes I paid for.
He stood, looked at the paper as if it were a mild weather report, and said, “I would prefer not to.”
I smiled, thinking it a joke.
It was not.
He returned to his desk and continued copying other pages as if preference were a law written above our letterhead.
The phrase became his architecture.
Proofreading?
He would prefer not to.
Errands to the notary across Sixth?
Prefer not.
Joining a call with a nervous client?
Prefer not.
Leaving at closing when the cleaners arrived with their carts?
Prefer not—he remained, a gray shape in the after-hours fluorescence, eating nothing I could see.
When I asked where he lived, he preferred not to say.
I discovered, one Sunday when I came in for a forgotten flash drive, that he lived in the office.
A thin blanket folded under the desk.
A plastic cup.
A phone that never lit.
Soap from the common bathroom.
I tried reason, then charity, then irritation.
I offered other duties, a different desk, even money to leave quietly and start elsewhere.
Each time the same soft sentence, delivered without anger, without plea, without the courtesy of explanation.
Clients noticed the stillness behind the screen and glanced at me as if I were keeping a ghost on payroll.
I felt, absurdly, that Bartleby had become the office’s true center, and the rest of us orbited his refusal.
At last I moved the practice to another floor in the same building and left him there with a sealed note and cash on his blotter.
The landlord called within a week.
Bartleby had remained.
Security walked past him and then around him.
He was removed to the Tombs—yes, still called that by the older clerks—where the walls were not soft and preference meant nothing to anyone with keys.
I visited because not visiting felt like a second abandonment.
He stood in the yard facing a wall the color of wet newspaper.
When I spoke his name he did not turn.
A grub-man laughed and said the man would prefer not to dine.
I pressed money into a hand that smelled of metal and asked that Bartleby be fed anyway.
Later I found him lying in the yard near the base of the wall, knees drawn, eyes open to nothing that included me.
The grub-man shrugged.
“He’s asleep.”
He was not asleep.
I left the prison and walked toward the park as evening came down between the buildings.
For a long time I could not shake the mildness of his voice, how it had asked for nothing and taken everything, including the part of me that believed a gentle workplace could always find a door.
